idiom_name: def with yield / generator expressions / itertools (islice, count, takewhile)
implementation_notes: Python makes laziness a language feature: any function containing yield returns a generator that suspends with its frame intact, generator expressions build anonymous lazy sequences, and itertools supplies the iterator algebra (count, islice, takewhile, chain, groupby) documented as fast, memory-efficient building blocks; range and the dict view objects are lazy sequences too. Generators are single-use and unmemoized, so repeated traversal needs a factory function or an explicit cache (functools.lru_cache, itertools.tee); a hand-written iterator class remains justified when the position must be inspected, reset or serialised.
code_sketch:
from itertools import islice

def fib():
    a, b = 0, 1
    while True:                       # infinite, lazy
        yield a
        a, b = b, a + b

evens = (n for n in fib() if n % 2 == 0)
print(list(islice(evens, 10)))        # forces exactly ten elements
pitfalls: A generator is exhausted after one pass: reuse silently produces an empty sequence (often the cause of a 'missing elements' bug), so APIs should return a fresh generator per call.
Materializing operations (list(), sorted(), sum(), len() on a generator) consume the whole source and hang forever on an infinite one; bound with islice/takewhile first.
Generator cleanup only runs when the frame is closed: abandoned generators delay file/connection release until GC, and catching GeneratorExit (or yielding inside finally) breaks the close protocol.

variants.name: Async generators (PEP 525)
variants.idiom_name: async def with yield, consumed by async for and closed with aclose()
variants.implementation_notes: An async generator is declared async def with yield: it may await inside the body and is pulled with async for or anext(), so I/O-bound element production applies backpressure by awaiting each pull and task cancellation reaches the suspended frame; aclose() (plus the event loop's shutdown hooks) runs the async cleanup path. It replaces the synchronous generator only when elements genuinely await something, and it is still single-consumer and unmemoized.
variants.code_sketch:
async def tail(path):
    async with aiofiles.open(path) as f:
        async for line in f:
            yield line.rstrip("\n")    # one line per awaited pull

async for line in tail("app.log"):
    if "ERROR" in line:
        break                          # aclose() runs the cleanup path
pitfalls: Async generators are finalised through the event loop: relying on garbage collection (no async with/aclosing) leaves sockets and tasks pending and emits warnings.
Two tasks cannot consume one async generator concurrently - interleaved anext() calls steal elements - so shared streams need a queue or a single consumer.
Unlike synchronous generators, closing requires an await (aclose), so callers that only break out of async for hand cleanup to the loop's async-generator hooks.
